caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1241 of 2001
lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Senior Advocate, Rafique-ul-Huq, Senior Advocate with him), instructed by Sufia Khatun, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioner. 

Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate, instructed by Chowdhury Md Zahangir, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent No. 4. 

Not represented—Respondent Nos. 1-3.
parties:
Rajkumari Unika Devi ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: Rajkumari Unika Devi, the adopted daughter of late Mong Chief Raja Mong Prue Sain of Manikchari, Chittagong Hill Tracts seeks leave to appeal against the impugned judgment and order dated 21st August 2000 passed in Writ Petition No. 3466 of 1998 discharging the Rule against the impugned notification dated 26-10-1998 appointing respondent No. 4 Paillya Prue Chowdhury as the Chief of Mong Circle (Mong Chief) under the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulations and directing the Commissioner, Chittagong Division to arrange investiture under regulation 48 of the said Regulation. The petitioner Rajkumari Unika Devi challenged the said appointment stating, inter alia, that the said respondent No. 4 was earlier appointed as the Mong Chief on 30-1-1991 by the then Government, on temporary basis and the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 344 of 1991 before the High Court Division against his such appointment. By judgment and order dated 4-9-1995 in the said Writ Petition (reported in 1996 BLD 408 ) the appointment of respondent No. 4 (who was respondent No. 5 in the said Writ Petition) was declared illegal and the said respondent No. 4 did not prefer any appeal before the Appellate Division. The petitioner came to know about the aforesaid appointment of respondent No. 4 for the first time from a report published in the daily Ittefaq on 29th October, 1998. No copy of the said memo was served on the petitioner though she is entitled to be appointed as the Mong Chief. The petitioner then filed an application to the respondent No. 1 for her appointment which is still pending before the respondent No. 1. The case of the petitioner is that she is the daughter of late Mong Prue Saine, the late Mong Chief of the Mong Circle of Chittagong Hill Tracts. After marriage, the petitioner along with her husband moved into the residential palace of the Mong Chief during the lifetime of her father late Mong Prue Sain and since then she has been living there as one of the member of the family of the Mong Raja. The petitioner's further case is that Rani Nihar Bala Devi, (mother of the petitioner) who was a daughter of the then Chakma Chief Raja Bhuban Mohan Roy, was appointed as Assistant Mong Chief on 20-9-1995 to help her husband late Mong Chief in performing his duties and functions. After the death of the late Mong Chief Mong Prue Sain in 1984 his wife Rani Nihar Bala was also appointed on 11-10-1984 as acting Chief of Mong Circle by the then Government till the appointment of the successor. The petitioner, who is the only child of late Mong Chief, was a matriculate. During her father's time, she was appointed as Headman of Mauza 215- Dabal Chari by the Deputy Commissioner. She discharged her functions for several years. Subsequently, she resigned from the said post. The petitioner used to assist her father late Mong Chief Raja Mong Prue Sain and her mother Rani Nihar Bala Devi in the administration of Mong Circle. 

 2. The petitioner, while narrating the history of the Mong Raja family, disclosed that the Mong Chief is commonly known as Mong Raja. The Mong Raja family is of Arakanese Mong descent being the descendants of the Royal family of Arakan who came to Chittagong Hill Tracts in the 16th century and they are Burmese Mong by caste. The Chief of the Mong Circle have always been appointed from the family of Mong Raja in accordance with the personal law, tradition, practice, customs and usage. A person who is not a member of Raj family cannot be appointed as the Mong Chief. In fact, all the Chiefs of all the circles in the Chittagong Hill Tracts namely, Chakma, Bhomong and Mong, are being appointed from amongst the members of the respective Raj families. The Chittagong Hill Tracts was constituted a separate district by Act XII of 1900. After the death of Mong Raja Kongjoy in 1826 his minor son Mong Raja Keoja Sain became the Mong Chief at the age of 7 years and during his minority a cousin of his acted as the guardian till 1840 when Keoja Sain coming of age took over that Chiefship himself. After the death of Mong Raja Keoja Sain his son Mong Raja Narabadi succeeded his father in 1870. Mong Raja Narabadi had no male issue, who died in 1879 leaving behind two minor daughters, Chuti and Hala Marsong. Raja Narabadi was succeeded by his younger brother Mong Raja Keoja Prue in 1879. The said Keoja Prue before becoming the Mong Chief had all along been living in the same mess and same building with his elder brother Narabadi as a member of family of the Mong Chief. 

 3. The said infant daughters of Raja Narabadi were brought up by him. Mong Raja Kheoja Sain died in 1883 and had no male issue. He left behind his widow who remarried an ordinary tribal man against the wishes of other members of the Raj family and, as such, she was excluded from the Raj family. Mong Raja Kheoja Sain was succeeded by his sister's son Mong Raja Nephru Sain in 1884. He was the second son of Pomai, the eldest daughter of Mong Raja Kheoja. As the said Mong Raja Kheoja Sain had no male issue the then Deputy Commissioner Mr Forbes visited Manik Chari and consulted with the members and other well-wishers of the Raj family and after due consideration he concurred with the members of the Raj family and their well-wishers that Raja Neprue Sain would succeed Raja Kheoja Prue Sain as the Mong Chief. The first son of Pomai being illiterate and too old to be imparted any training and education, the second son of Neprue Sain was nominated and proclaimed as future Chief of Mong Circle in 1884 when he was only 12 years old. According to the custom, he was taken into the Mong Raja residence and he began to live in the same mess and in the same building along with other members of the Raj family. During the minority of Mong Raja Nephrue Sain, the estate was under the Court of Wards and after attaining majority in 1893 he was installed as the Chief of Mong Circle. After his proclamation as the Mong Chief, Raja Nephrue Sain married Rani Chuti and Rani Halamraso, both daughters of his maternal uncle late Raja Narabadi. The said Mong Raja had no male issue but had a daughter named Raj Kumari Nanoomah, and she was married to Prince Konghla, the younger son of the then Bohmong Chief Raja Chaila Prue. Prince Konghla was a student at that time. After marriage he gave up all connection with his entire family and moved to the residence of Mong Raja Nephrue Sain. 

 4. Rajkumari Nanooma got two sons by Prince Khongla, who died very young. Prince Konghla also died in 1915. After the death of Mong Raja Nephrue Sain, Rajkumari Nanooma being the heir of her father became the Chief of the Mong Circle. After her death in 1951 her son Kumar Mong Prue Sain (father of the petitioner) became the Chief in 1954; on the death of Mong Prue Sain in 1984 his wife Nihar Bala Devi became the Chief of the Mong Circle. The above genealogy vide Annexure G is a family tree of Mong Raj family. The family history of the Mong Raja was maintained in the office of the respondent No. 2 where the history of Mong Raja, together with customs, practice, tradition and usage of the succession are also recorded. Besides, a report called 'Mills' report and reply to the then Secretary of Bengal by the Tribal Chiefs also contained the history, tradition, customs, usage, practice of succession, etc. relating to the Tribal Chiefs and Raj families of Chittagong Hill Tracts. 

 5. Under the tradition, customs and usages of the Mong Circle, those who do not and cannot live in the same mess and in the same building with the Mong Raja and the principal members of the Mong Raja's family are not treated as the members of the Mong Raj family, however, much they may claim the relationship. Thus the relatives not having been living in the same mess with Mong Raja are not considered to the claim of Chiefship and, as such, no concession or allowance is given to such a relation. 

 6. Further case of the petitioner is that in the event of there being no direct male heir, the succession follows in the female line. In case of Mong Chiefship, the succession follows according to the long standing principles of customs, tradition, practice and usage. The consultation with the members of the Raj family is the only custom and the consent or approval of the members of the Raj family is the only element of the right to succession to the Chiefship of the Mong Circle. The appointment of Rajkumari Nanoomah, the daughter of late Mong Raja Nephrue Sain as Mong Chief was by a notification published in Calcutta Gazette dated 14th May, 1936 (Annexure H). The Mill's report (Annexure I) confirmed and reiterated that according to law of inheritance, tradition, usage and customs the succession in case of the Mong Chiefship follows in the direct male line or in the female line in case there is no direct male line and the said practice has always been observed from generation to generation. Late Raja Mong Prue Sain was the only child of his parents. He had no brother or sister. The respondent No. 4 is not his relative not to speak of being a brother's son. The respondent No. 4 is a total stranger to the family of late Mong Chief as he was born and brought up at Khagrachhari which is about 30 miles away from Manikchari which is the place where the Mong Raja comes from and- lives and his residence and palace located. 

 7. The petitioner's further case is that, there is a deed of determination (Will) which was executed by late Raja Mong Prue Sain during his lifetime on 9-7-1967 and the said Will provided that after his death his wife Rani Nihar Bala Devi would be appointed Mong Raja in his place and after her death, his daughter Rajkumari Unika Devi (the writ petitioner) would be the Raja of the Mong Circle. The petitioner is therefore, the lawful heir to the Mong Chiefship in accordance with law of inheritance, tradition, practice, customs and also according to the said Will of late Raja. 

 8. There are precedents of Raja's daughter or wife from another Tribal family becoming the Chief such as Rajkumari Nanooma became the Mong Chief after the death of her father Mong Raja Nephrue Sain, and Rani Nihar Bala Devi became the Chief after the death of her husband Mong Raja Mong Prue Sain. There is also the precedent of son-in-law from another Tribal family becoming a member of the family when he moved into Raj family in their house after marriage with the Princess and becoming Raja upon succession. Hence the petitioner's husband is also entitled to and qualified under the law, customs, tradition, and usage to be appointed as the Mong Chief. Apart from this, the petitioner is entitled under the law, customs, tradition and usage as well as by dint of the will to succeed Rani Nihar Bala and Raja Mong Prue Sain as the Mong Chief after their death. 

 9. The respondent No. 1 having acted contrary to the aforesaid law, will customs, usage, traditions, convention and without consulting the family of the Mong Chief, on 30-1-1991 had temporarily appointed respondent No. 4 as the Mong Chief till the successor of the Mong Chief was appointed (Annexure M). 

 10. The petitioner thereupon made representation to the respondent Nos. 1-3 for appointing her as the Mong Chief as per law, traditions, customs, usage and as per will on the death of Rani Nihar Bala Devi but without any avail. The petitioner and her husband Rajib Roy Chowdhury being eligible under the law and customs to become the Mong Chief filed Writ Petition No. 344 of 1991 before the High Court Division challenging the temporary appointment of respondent No. 4 as Mong Chief. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute on 4-9-1995 holding that such appointment should be made in compliance with the relevant laws, traditions, convention, customs, practice and usage involving the appointment of Mong Chief. 

 11. The Rule was contested by the Government respondent No. 1 as well as by respondent No. 4 filing separate affidavits-in-opposition. The respondent No. 1 denying the material allegations stated, inter alia, that the petitioner is not the daughter of late Raja Mong Prue Sain and she has nothing to be aggrieved by appointment of respondent No. 4 as the Chief of Mong Circle and his appointment has been rightly done by the Government in view of the judgment in Writ Petition No. 488 of 1991 (1996 BLD 406 = 1 BLC 555) and in compliance of the relevant laws, traditions, convention, customs and practice of the Mong Circle. The questions involved in the said writ petition before the High Court Division and the cited decision of the Appellate Division in 50 DLR (AD) 73 are not the same as in the instant writ petition. It is to be noted that appointments of Mong Chief and the Bhomong Chief do not stand on the same footing. In Bhomong Circle the eldest living member of the blood connected descendants of the Raj family is appointed as Bhomong Chief whereas in the Mong Circle the son of the Chief will be the Mong Chief and in the absence of male line the Chiefship may also go to the female line having blood connection and the tradition is being followed consistently in the Mong Circle. The petitioner is not the daughter of late Raja Mong Prue Sain of the Mong Circle of Chittagong Hill Tracts. The late King brought the petitioner, gave her shelter at the palace and brought her up under his care but she, having no blood connection with the late Raja, cannot be treated as a member of Raj family under law, customs and tradition of the Mong Circle as recognised by the Government. The husband of the petitioner Rajib Roy Chowdhury is not a member of Mong Circle who is from Chakma Circle. No one of different tribe/circle staying in the same mess can claim as member of the Raj family under the law, tradition and customs of the Mong Circle. The petitioner was clearly described as the adopted daughter of said late Mong Raja Mong Prue Sain in the will executed by said Mong Raja. Knowing fully well that she is not the daughter of the late Raja she has falsely claimed herself as the daughter of Raja Mong Prue Sain and she cannot be said to be the real child. The mere appointment of a person as the headman does not entitle him/her to be appointed as the Mong Chief. To become a Mong Chief one must have blood connection with the Mong Raja and this is the tradition, customs and usage of the Mong Circle. The so-called will allegedly executed by Raja has got no legal footing and the Government has never recognised the so-called will. There is no law, traditions or customs to appoint a male or female who was given shelter and brought up in the Mong Raja family to be appointed as the Mong Chief. The Government never acted arbitrarily in appointing the respondent No. 4 as Chief of the Mong Circle having blood connection with the late Raja Mong Prue Sain and also keeping in view the tradition, customs, practice and usage of the Mong Circle. The Chief of Mong Circle was always selected from the blood connected descendent of the Mong Raja. The petitioner being an adopted daughter of late Raja had no blood connection either from the male or female side of the Mong Raja family even if she lived with her husband in the palace and cannot claim to be a member of the Raj family. The petitioner's husband is a man of different tribe and has no blood connection with Mong Raja late Mong Prue Sain and, as such, he has also no right to be appointed as Mong Chief. The respondent No. 4 is not a stranger in the family of late Mong Chief. The late Mong Raja Nephrue Chai Chowdhury was the grandfather of late Raja Mong Prue Sain. The said Nephrue Chai Chowdhury had a younger brother named Kala Chand who had a son named Aparna Charan Chowdhury who died leaving one son named Kea-Swe Chowdhury who is still alive and he being the living heir of Mong Chief but because of his old age he nominated his son respondent No. 4 Paillya Prue Chowdhury to be appointed as Mong Chief. The Government considered this aspect of the case of the respondent No. 4. 

 12. Regarding the petitioner's statement that there are precedents of Raja's daughter or wife from another tribal family becoming the Chief are not correct. The fact is that the daughter of Mong Chief Rajkumari Nanoomah who became the Mong Raja was the daughter of Nephru Sain. Rani Nihar Bala Devi was made acting Mong Chief and not the Mong Chief. She was allowed only to discharge the function of the Mong Chief showing respect that she is the widow of late Raja till the appointment of a successor to the late Mong Chief. The son-in-law Nephrue Sain who became the Mong Chief had blood connection with the late Mong Raja Narabadi as has been stated by the petitioner himself in this writ petition. Till date no one has been appointed as the Mong Chief who had no blood connection with Raj family. The respondent No. 4 had already been installed/investitured as the Mong Chief by holding a installation ceremony on 27-10-1998 at a function held in the Town Hall, Khagrachhari by the Divisional Commissioner Chittagong and thereby the appointment of respondent No. 4 has already been given affect to. 

 13. The petitioner not being an heir of Mong Raja, the Deputy Commissioner, Khagrachhari, respondent No. 3, acted rightly in not issuing succession certificate in her favour. It is not understood as to why the petitioner who claimed to be a member of Mong Raj family being the resident of Manik Chari under District Khagrachhari did apply for issuing a succession certificate to the Deputy Commissioner Rangamati as under the law the proper authority is the Deputy Commissioner, Khagrachhari to issue such certificate and not the Deputy Commissioner, Rangamati and, as such, the petitioner cannot take any benefit/advantage from the succession certificate issued by the Deputy Commissioner, Rangamati. It is further stated that Government is not obliged to consult the Chief of all the circles before making any appointment of Mong Chief. The matter of appointment of the Mong Chief was thoroughly inquired into by the Deputy Commissioner, Khagrachhari and the report was given to the effect that respondent No. 4 has got blood connection with the late Mong Chief, Raja Mong Prue Sain. It is further stated that the petitioner being a Hindu lady and her husband being Chakma, the identity and heritage of the Mong Circle will be extinguished altogether if the petitioner or her husband is appointed as the Mong Chief. The respondent No. 4 has been appointed as the Mong Chief lawfully as he is a man of Mong Circle having blood connection with the late Mong Raja. For the above reasons the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 14. The respondent No. 4 as well has contested the Rule stating, inter alia, that the petitioner has no reason to be aggrieved by his appointment as the Mong Chief. The question involved in the earlier writ petition and that of the present writ petition is not the same. In the earlier writ petition this respondent No. 4 was appointed Mong Chief on temporary basis and now the Government after thorough inquiry considered the case of the writ petitioner as well as of the respondent No. 4 and also considered the tradition, convention, customs and practice of Mong Circle and thereafter, appointed the respondent No. 4 as a descendent of Late Raja Mong Prue Sain being his maternal cousin's son. In the Biographical Encyclopedia of notable families in Pakistan (Annexure C to the Writ Petition) the petitioner was described as the only daughter of late Raja Mong Prue Sain when admittedly she is the adopted daughter and, as such, shoe cannot become the real child of late Mong Prue Sain. Furthermore, the fact remains that both the petitioner and her husband had no blood connection with the Mong Raja in any way. There is no customs, traditions and usage prevailing in the Mong Circle that Mong Chief could nominate someone to succeed him or her as the Mong Chief through a will as has been claimed by the petitioner in the writ petition and, as such, the testamentary disposition by will is not legal and valid being contrary to law, custom, tradition and usage since the petitioner admittedly is an adopted daughter having no blood connection with Mong Raja. The respondent No. 4 has categorically asserted that he is the maternal cousin's son of late Raja Mong Prue Sain. Being the maternal cousin's son as per family tree (Annexure 2 of the affidavit-in-opposition) respondent No. 4 is eligible and also under the customs, tradition practice and usage to become Chief of the Mong Circle. There is no material to show that one was ever appointed as the Mong Chief simply because one lived in the Raj Bari and took meal in the same mess. The respondent No. 4 further stated that Nephnie Sain was appointed as Mong Chief as he was descendant of the Raj family and had blood connection with Mong Raja Kheoja Prue Sain. Since the respondent No. 4 is the maternal cousin's son of late Raja Mong Prue Sain he is a blood descendent and is eligible to be appointed as the Mong Chief as per law, customs, traditions, practices and usage. This respondent is not a total stranger to the family of Mong Chief Late Mong Prue Sain as alleged by the petitioner. To be appointed as Mong Chief it is not necessary that one must be inhabitant of Manikchari as contended by the petitioner. The customs, tradition and usage of Mong Circle is that to become Mong Chief one has to be the descendant of late Mong Raja having blood connection and in the instant case this respondent being blood connected with the late Mong Chief has been rightly appointed as Mong Chief by the Government. The Government having inquired into the matter rightly appointed the respondent No. 4 as Mong Chief and has done no illegality nor violated any law, traditions and customs and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 16. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, contended that succession to Mong Chiefship follows the long standing customs, traditions, practices and usage and it is done in consultation with the members of Raj family and, as such, the consent of the members of Raj family is a pre-condition to the succession as enjoined by the provision of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulations, 1990 and therefore, argued that the respondent No. 1 acted illegally and without lawful authority in appointing the respondent No. 4 as the Mong Chief violating the provisions of the Regulations, 1900 and the long standing practice, tradition, customs and usages. 

 17. The learned Counsel for the petitioner further submitted that the deed of determination (will) executed on 9-7-1967 provided that after his death his wife Rani Nihar Bala Devi would be appointed Mong Raja in his place and after her death his daughter (the petitioner herein), legal heir to the Mong Chiefship would be the Raja of the Mong Circle in accordance with the laws of inheritance, tradition, customs and usages and as such the respondent No. 1 instead of following the hereditary line of succession acted illegally in appointing the respondent No. 4 as the Mong Chief and thus has jeopardised the properties of Mong Rajas family being alienated to an outsider (respondent No. 4) depriving the petitioner of her right to inherit the family property and, as such, the impugned order is violative of Article 42 of the Constitution. 

 18. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Counsel appearing with Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, has joined the issue in submitting that the appointment of Mong Chief under rule 48 has been done without any lawful authority as the rule referred to is applicable in the case of the appointment of headman whereas the Mong Chief is being appointed on the basis of the recommendation of the Deputy Commissioner considering the tradition of the tribe/Mong Circle. 

 19. Mr Huq has referred to a genealogy in Annexure G to show that Kala Chand, the predecessor-in-interest of respondent No. 2, was neither the relation of the Mong King so as to entitle his heir respondent No. 4 become the Mong Chief inasmuch as respondent No. 4 never lived in the same Mahal under the same roof and mess with the late Mong Chief so as to entitle him to be the successor of the Mong Chief, on the contrary Raj Kumari who is admittedly an adopted daughter of the Mong Chief, she both under the law of succession and the will of late King was entitled to be appointed as a Chief of Mong Circle as per custom, usage and tradition of the tribe/Mong Circle. 

 20. Khondakar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent No. 4, submitted that although the adoption under the Buddhist law is applicable to the Mong Circle but the petitioner though could succeed to the personal properties of the late King on adoption but does not entitle her to be the Mong Chief, according to the custom, usage and tradition of the said Circle. Mr Ahmed next submits that there is no bar for a relation of a Mong Chief to be Chief of Mong Circle even if he has not resided under the same roof or in the same mess but the requirement of residence under the roof and dining at the same mess was for the sole purpose that the Mong Chief having earned a small amount of money and it is not possible to provide maintenance to other relations who were living outside the roof and in a separate mess. Mr Ahmed next submitted that all the three members of the Parliament from the Hill District and the headmen of the locality have recommended the appointment of respondent No. 4 as the Mong Chief according to the custom, tradition and usage of the Mong Circle. Mr Ahmed has further submitted that the petitioner has no legal right to claim to be the Chief of Mong Circle as she had no blood relation with the late Mong Chief or the family as required under the custom, tradition and practice and more so, admittedly the petitioner is a Hindu lady adopted as a daughter by the late Mong Chief and married to a Chakma who is not a Mong and against whom the late King had reservation. 

 21. Previously the Government had temporarily appointed the respondent No. 4 by order in Memo No. 40-Goh: (confirmation) dated 30-1-1991 to act as the Mong Chief asking the Office Assistant of late Rani Nihar Bala Devi to hand over the charge of Mong Chief to respondent No. 4 which was challenged by the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 344 of 1991 claiming that the petitioner was entitled in law to succeed late Rani Nihar Bala Devi but the Government has illegally issued the said memo which is liable to be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority. The Rule was made absolute holding that: 

 "Let us now see whether the order giving appointment to the respondent No. 5 as the Mong Chief pending final appointment to an eligible person as the Mong Chief has affected the right of the petitioner or not. The appointment though said to be made on temporary basis direction for making over charge to the appointee vide Annexure A1 before the finalisation of the application and determination of the claim of the petitioner No. 1 to became the Mong Chief according to laws, traditions, customs and practices prevailing amongst the tribe, in our view, has affected the right of the petitioners in getting her case considered by the appropriate authority. The appointment of respondent No. 5 though said to be temporary, as the Mong Chief with a direction to hand over the charge to the respondent No. 5 has practically had the effect of deciding the dispute once and for all leaving no room for consideration of the case of the petitioner and thus has caused serious anomalies in the status, position and administration of the affairs of Mong Circle. 

 For the aforesaid reasons, we are of the view that the order appointing the respondent No. 5 on a temporary basis as the Mong Chief till the finalisation of the matter involving the appointment of the Mong Chief from amongst eligible persons cannot be sustained and, therefore, the order vide Annexure A regarding the temporary appointment and the order vide Annexure A1 for handing over of the office to the local Upazila Nirbahi Officer is hereby declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. In view of the above the order of appointment of the respondent No. 5 and direction to hand over the charge of Mong Chiefship could not be sustained and hereby declared as being done without lawful authority but the respondents will be free to decide the matter of appointment of Mong Chief on consideration of the application filed by the petitioners vis-a-vis the claim of the respondent No. 5 or any person interested and eligible for appointment according to and in compliance of the relevant laws, traditions, convention, customs, practices of the Mong circle involving the appointment of Mong Chief in succession to late Raja Mong Prue Sain on regular basis." 

 22. The petitioner is admittedly a Hindu lady who was adopted by the Mong Chief as his daughter and according to law of adoption applicable to a Brumes and Buddhist, a Brumes Buddhist could adopt a child and in an adoption the maternal parents waive their right to inherit their child's estate and the adoptive parents confer on the adopted child the right to inherit their estate. So, the adoption is in the nature of a contract and, according to law on succession, when there are no maternal lineal descendants or even a Killima adopted child, an apatitha adopted child who lived with the deceased adopted parent shall inherit one half of the estate of the deceased along with the next of kins of the deceased person (Ms Than Nyus vs Baw Shwe Thit 14 Ran 557). Admittedly, the Mong Chief had no issue to inherit the deceased Mong Chief but has adopted the petitioner and, according to the law of adoption applicable to the late Mong Chief, she is entitled to inherit the left over personal properties/estate of the late Mong Chief as aforesaid. 

 23. But in the instant case though she is entitled to inherit the estate of late Mong Chief now the question remains as to whether she is entitled to inherit the post of the Mong Chief? The late King Mong Prue Sain has also expressed his desire by way of Will dated 9-7-1967 that his adopted daughter would be appointed to inherit him as the Chief of Mong Circle. 

 24. But, contrary to the desire of the late Mong Chief, the Government has issued the impugned notification appointing respondent No. 4 as the Mong Chief. 

 48. Investiture of the Chief and Appointment and Dismissal of Headmen. The investiture of the Chief is regulated by he Bengal Government. The headman will be appointed by the Deputy Commissioner in consultation with the Chiefs; they may be dismissed by the Deputy Commissioner for incompetence or misconduct after a reference to the Chief concerned. The Deputy Commissioner will not be bound in either case by the wishes of the Chief, but full consideration should be given to them. This appointment is not hereditary, but a son, where competent, may be appointed to succeed his father. 

 27. On perusal of the said rule it appears that the said rule does not provide the procedure for appointment of Chief of the Mong Circle except by stating that the investiture of the Chief is regulated by the Bengal Government though the said provision provides for appointment and dismissal of headmen. The said rule mentions about investiture of the Mong Chief by the Government only upon his appointment. Thus, in the absence of any legal provision for appointment of Chief of Mong Circle, let us examine what customs, usages and tradition are prevalent for the Mong Circle for appointment of the Mong Chief. 

 30. It appears from the resolution that the Government in Council has accepted the recommendation of the Commissioner of Chittagong Division who is the ex-officio Chief Executive of the Division under Chittagong Hill Tract Regulations 1900 and approved the succession of Srijakta Nanoomah to the office and dignity of the Mong Raja. Thus though Chittagong Hill Tracts Resolution or Rules for the Administration of Chittagong Hill Tracts do not provide any procedure for appointment or succession to the post of Mong Chief but by way of a custom, usage and practice that was prevalent requiring the recommendation as to appointment of Mong Chief by the Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong duly accepted and approved by the Governor in Council. 

 31. Annexure I to the writ petition being the memo No. 1086 dated 21st/22nd January 1929 issued by the Secretary to the Government of Bengal (Chtg) that one Mr Mills, a Special Officer was deputed in 1926 to advise Government regarding the status and duties of the Chiefs of Chittagong Hill Tracts who submitted his report in 1927. 

 32. It appears from "Mills" report forwarded to Mong King and the three Chiefs of the Chittagong Hill Tracts dated 21/22 January 1929, inter alia, that: 

 "The Mong Raja has properties in the regulation District of Chittagong besides those of Chittagong Hill Tracts. According to the Law of inheritance, traditions and customs the succession follows in the direct male line or in the female line in case when there is no direct male line. This practice has always been observed from generation to generation in the case of the Mong Chiefship. As the succession is made in the above ways no dispute ever arose with regard to the Chiefship of the Mong Circle. Up to Mong Raja Keojafru the succession followed in the male line but as Keojafru had no male issue, the succession followed in the female line. These principles hold good in all cases and the Deputy Commissioner Mr Stevens in supporting this principle observed in 1925. "According to the customs of the Palengtsa Maghs she (Mong Rajah's daughter Raj Kumari Nanoomah) is her father's heir and should the occasion ever arise, she will certainly be fitted to do this work". The Chiefship is hereditary and so the title "Mong Raja" is a hereditary title of the Mong Chief (vide page 415 of the Imperial Gazetteer of India. Provincial Series 1999)." "Mong Rajah is a descendant of the king of Arrakan. Mong Raja Gri itself was the title of the king of Arrakan. Mong Raja is thus commonly known as the Mong Raja (Para 6 of Commissioner Lord Ulick Browne's No. 421 dated 12-11-1968). As Bohmong Gri is the title of the Bohmong Chief so also Man Rajah Gri is the title of the Mong Chief. Being a member of the royal family of Arrakan Mong Chief had with him the title of Mong Raja Gri. The title "Mong Raja" was thus recognised by Government as the "hereditary" title of the Mong Chief (vide page 415 of the Imperial Gazetteer of India Provincial Series 1909). Those who were unaware of the past history of the Mong Chieftainship might have recorded something on superficial information. The correspondence of 1892 appear to have taken place at the time of the present Mong Raja but he was not aware of it. Thus the wordings that "Keojasain was accorded the title of Mong Raja by the voice of the people" have no foundation in it at all. He ruled from 1849 to January 1870 and it is impossible that he should be so described long after his death. It will appear from page 36 of Captain Lewin's "Hill Tracts of Chittagong" that the Kyangtha villagers living on the north of the Karnafully river acknowledged the supremacy of the Mong Raja. Thus Mong Raja was not a clan Chief but the Chief over the Kyangthas to the north of the Karnafully river." "Among the Maghs, in the event of there being no direct male heir, the successions follows in the female line with the exception of the Chieftainship of the Bohmong in which the succession to the next eldest male blood relative and does not follow in the direct line (page 33 of Eastern Bengal and Assam District Gazetteer, Chittagong Hill Tracts). In the case of Mong Chieftainship, the succession should therefore take place according to Law of inheritance, principles and customs in order to upkeep of the prestige and position of the Raj family clan selection. Mong Raja Keojafru died in July 1883 and there being no male heir, the present Mong Raja succeeded his maternal uncle in 1884. Thus there being no direct male heir, the succession followed in the female line. This example holds good in the case of his successor as well  "According to the custom of the Palengtsa Maghs She (Raj Kumari Nanoomah, the eldest daughter of the Mong Chief) is her father's heir and should the occasion ever arise, she will certainly be filled to do his work". 

 33. From the above, it is apparent that according to the law of inheritance, tradition and customs the succession to the post of Mong Chief follows in the direct male line and in case of no male issue it follows in the direct female line, thus making the succession to the Chiefship as hereditary and the late Mong Raja is thus the hereditary title of the Mong Chief. It further appears that Mong Keojafru who died in July 1883 was not survived by any male heir and in that event he was succeeded by his maternal uncle in 1884. Thus in the absence of any heir to succeed the hereditary title of the Mong Chief, the succession would go to the other male relation of the late Mong Raja even of the female line. 

 34. It further appears that where there is no direct descendant, the Chief of Mong Circle could be appointed from one of his blood relations if there be any. Thus the succession to the office of the Mong Chief of the Mong Circle is governed by the law of inheritance, customs and principles from its heirs and relations in keeping up of the prestige and dignity of the Raj family. 

 35. The Chief of the Mong Circle was always selected from the blood connected descendants of the late Mong Chief and admittedly the petitioner has no such blood connection from either male or female side of the family of the Mong Chief and thus is not legally entitled to be appointed as the Mong Chief and there is no such custom, usage, tradition or practice to appoint an outsider as the Mong Chief. 

 36. Annexure 6(a) to the Affidavit-in-Opposition go to show that admittedly the late Mong Chief Mong Prue Sain Chowdhury died issueless but one Kala Chand Chowdhury was the brother of 4th Mong King Nephrue Sain Chowdhury who is survived, amongst others, by one Aparna Charan Chowdhury who died leaving Kasau Chowdhury, the father of respondent No. 4 Paillaya Prue Chowdhury. The said genealogy though denied by the petitioner relying on Annexure G to the writ petition but genealogy in Annexure G is not supported by any other papers, on the contrary, Annexure 6(a) finds support in other papers including Annexure 2, the summary prepared by the Minister of Hill Tracts Affairs placed before the Prime Minister and Annexure 5 a memo proposed by the Commissioner, Chittagong Division for the Ministry of Home Affairs in respect of appointment of Chief of Mong Circle stating, inter alia, that: 

 "This forces us to look for a natural successor to Raja Mong Prue Sain. We find that successor in the person of Mr Kusasu Chowdhury who is a direct descendant of the first Mong Chief. His grandfather Mr Kala Chand Chowdhury and the fourth Mong Chief Nefru Sain Chowdhury (grandfather of late Raja Mong Prue Sain) are own brothers. Mr Kasasu Chowdhury, however, is very old now as such he has allowed his son Mr Paillya Prue Chowdhury to claim the position of Mong Chief. A photocopy of the genealogical chart is enclosed at Annexure 'A' for rough reference. Considering the facts and circumstances stated above I feel that Mr Paillya Prue Chowdhury is the natural and lawful successor to the position of Mong Chief." 

 37. It further appears from Annexure X4 to the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent Nos. 1-3 that upon death of Mong Raja Keojafan who had no male issue, Nephru Sain, the son of eldest daughter of the late King, was considered to be the rightful heir to succeed the office of the Mong Chief. 

 38. Thus from the above, it is clear that the appointment of the Mong Chief of the Mong Circle in the absence of any direct descendant of the late Mong Chief was from either male or female side, out of a man or woman claiming related and having blood connection with the late Mong Chief and such person could be the Mong Chief according to the law of inheritance, principles and customs in upkeep with the prestige and dignity of the Raj family. 

 39. Now coming to the question to what extent the customs, tradition and usages have the effect on the succession to the position of the Mong Chief? The 'Mills' reports provide that according to the customs of the Palengtsa Maghs she (Mong Raja's daughter Raj Kumari Nanoomuh) is her father's heir and if the occasion ever arise, she will certainly be fitted to do this work". Thus customs plays a predominant part in the matter of succession in the absence of any heir to the late Mong Chief. Customs in this case is the local customs of the Mong Chief which constitutes a source of law for the Mong Circle in the absence of any law as regards succession. Thus customs is something that has the effect of local law. 

 42. It is clear from the discussion above that it is the custom, usage and tradition of the Mong Circle that in case of appointment of the Chief of Mong Circle in the absence of a male heir of the deceased King, the female heir of the late King is entitled to be the Mong Chief but in the absence of either of the two, a member of the family having blood connection shall be appointed to the office of the Mong Chief of the Mong Circle. 

 43. The petitioner has asserted that under the tradition, custom and usage of the Mong Circle, those who do not live in the same mess and in the same building with the Meng Chief are not treated as the members of the Mong Raj family, however, much they claim the relationship and, as such, the respondent No. 4 admittedly not being staying in the same mess and under the same roof is not treated to be member of the Mong Raj family so as to be appointed as the Mong Chief and has referred to Annexure L to the writ petition (the family history of Mong Raja as prepared by the political development of the Government of Bangladesh). 

 44. Now admittedly, the respondent No. 4 though a member of the family, was not living in the same mess and under the same roof with the late King. In view of the submission of Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed that successor of Mong Chief must be a person who has resided in the same building and in the same mess, Khondakar Mahbubuddin Ahmed has referred to Ext Al to the Affidavit-in-opposition which read as: 

 "In view of the smallness of the area and income of the Mong Raja's Circle separate allowances for the members of the Raj family cannot be allowed and so whoever be the Chief must, as a custom, have to live with the principal members of the Raj family in the residential building of the Mong Raja." As the surviving members of the Raj family live in the same building and in the same mess with the Mong Raja, question of payment of allowance to any member of the Raj family has never arisen." 

 45. The issue regarding members of the Raj family to live in the same mess and under same roof is directed to the question of payment of allowances to any member of the Raj family due to small area of Mong Raja's Circle. In the case of Mong Chieftainship, the succession follows according to the law of inheritance and long standing principle of customs together with the consultation with the members of the Raj family. Thus, it cannot be said that those who do not live with Mong Chief in the same mess and under the same roof are not members of the Raj family and, as such, the respondent No. 4 though was not entitled to the payment of allowances on ground of living in separate mess and roof than the Mong Chief but cannot be termed to be not a member of the Raj family. 

 46. It further appears from Annexure II, the genealogy showing respondent No. 4 to be the heir of late Kasasu Chowdhury and being the only available and able competent successor, has also been recommended to be the competent person to become the Mong Chief by all the other members of the family including the father of the respondent No. 4, three members of the Parliament of the three Hill Districts, almost all the Mong Chiefs, the Chairmen of the Local Union Parishads and other concerned association within the Kingdom. 

 47. Furthermore, it appears from 'Mills' report that Man Rajah Gri is the title of the Mong Chief and that the title devolves as the hereditary title of the Mong Chief. Thus only a blood relation, however, remote it may be, if found to be competent and recommended by all concerned of the Raj family and the authorities concerned including the Divisional/ Deputy Commissioner, a relation of the late Mong King either from male or female side is entitled to be appointed by the Government to the hereditary post of the Mong Chief and to hold the title. Therefore, the succession to the post of Mong Chief is to take place according to the law of inheritance, principle, customs and tradition in order to upkeep the prestige and dignity of the Raj family as detailed above. 

 48. It appears from Annexure IV to the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No. 4 that he has already been installed/investitured as the Mong Chief by holding an installation/ investiture ceremony on 27-10-1998 at a function held in the Town Hall at Khagrachhari by the Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong pursuant to the order of the Government dated 26-10-1998 and the function was attended by Chairman of the District Pariashad, Chairman Paurshava, Deputy Commissioner, Khagrachhari Police Super, elites and general public. Accordingly, the respondent No. 4 has been functioning as the Mong Chief of the Mong Circle. 

 49. From the above consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, law regarding succession to the post of the Chief of Mong Circle and the customs, traditions, usages and the recommendations by the Deputy Commissioner, three members of the Parliament from Hill Districts, Chairmen and headmen of the Hill District in consonance to the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulations, we do not find any illegality in the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division.
